newsitem.title: USA: New data show consumer inflation low, sales slow.
newsitem.headline: New data show consumer inflation low, sales slow.

text.p: Consumer prices inched up in August and retail sales advanced weakly, the government said Friday, adding more fuel to an already raging debate over whether the Federal Reserve should raise interest rates this month.

The Labour Department said the Consumer Price Index rose by just 0.1 percent last month, compared with a July increase of 0.3 percent. Sales at retail stores, up only 0.2 percent in a separate Commerce Department report, were far short of expectations.
The news gave many Wall Street forecasters the proof they needed to declare that inflation remains well under control.

"I continue to believe that inflation is not a problem," said Irwin Kellner, chief economist at Chase Manhattan. "The Fed has the economy right where it wants it -- growing just fast enough to stay out of recession but not fast enough to increase price pressures."
Wall Street has focused closely on the inflation figures as it tries to predict whether the Federal Reserve might find it necessary to raise interest rates when its top policy-makers meet Sept. 24.

"The people on the Fed who want to wait have some new ammunition to maybe more convincingly argue that case and perhaps win the day," said Stuart Hoffman, chief economist at PNC Bank Corp. in Pittsburgh.

Excluding the typically volatile food and energy components, the core rate of inflation also rose 0.1 percent. Wall Street forecasters had expected a rise of 0.2 percent in both the overall and the core CPI rate.

The inflation-sensitive U.S. Treasury market surged after the CPI report, with the benchmark 30-year bond soaring more than 1-1/2 points, pulling its yield well below 7.0 percent, to 6.94 percent from Thursday's 7.08 percent.
But some economists suggested that the Fed still may feel it needs to boost interest rates if it wants to ward off a pickup in inflation.

"Does the Fed have the luxury of waiting another couple of months to see how this shakes out?" asked Northern Trust Corp. economist Paul Kasriel. "It's obviously going to be a very spirited discussion."

In the consumer price report, food prices continued their upward march in August, jumping 0.4 percent following an increase of 0.5 percent in July. But energy prices fell 0.6 percent, paced by a steep 2.0 percent drop in gasoline prices.
Apparel and upkeep prices also fell sharply, down 1.4 percent, the biggest monthly decline since January 1949. Apparel prices were down only 0.1 percent in July.

Total retail sales rose 0.2 percent last month to a seasonally adjusted $205 billion -- well below Wall Street economists' forecasts of a 0.7 percent increase -- after a slight 0.1 percent gain in July.

During August, sales of new cars were up only 0.1 percent to $49.7 billion after being flat in July. New cars account for about one-fifth of total retail sales, so swings in demand strongly affect the overall monthly figures.
Excluding cars, retail sales rose 0.2 percent during each of July and August.

Domestic automakers previously reported brisk sales in August, which led analysts to anticipate a strong rise in overall monthly retail business. Some of the car dealers' sales data may not yet have been captured by the government's monthly survey.

The consumer price report followed the department's release Thursday of August producer price data showing that overall inflation at the wholesale level rose 0.3 percent, while the core rate fell 0.1 percent.
CPI housing prices were up 0.2 percent following a rise of 0.4 percent in July. New car prices were up 0.3 percent, while airline fares fell 0.3 percent.
Medical care posted an increase of 0.2 percent, compared with a 0.3 percent increase in July.
Recent data have showed tighter conditions in the job market, suggesting that employers will need to pay higher wages to attract certain types of workers.
Economists have feared that those higher labour costs could eventually be reflected in steeper prices at the cash register if businesses decide to pass them along to consumers.
